My work sits at the intersection of soil microbial ecology, biogeochemical cycling, and long-term agricultural management. I use sequencing-based approaches and wet-lab methods to understand how microbial communities drive nitrogen transformations in soil.

title: Research
text:
Methods I Use
Molecular: DNA/RNA extraction, 16S & nifH amplicon sequencing, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, qPCR, functional gene cloning
Statistical: R (vegan, phyloseq, ALDEx2), PCoA, NMDS, RDA, PERMANOVA, differential abundance analysis
Field: Soil sampling, gas flux measurement, camera trap deployment, point count bird surveys, acoustic recording

title: Home
text:
About
I am a PhD student in the Department of Biology at Saint Louis University, advised by Dr. Laibin Huang. My research focuses on nitrogen cycling in long-term agricultural ecosystems — specifically, how a century of differential crop rotation and fertilization has shaped soil microbial communities and nitrification-related processes in the Morrow Plots, the oldest continuously cultivated experimental field in the Americas.
I work with metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and 16S/nifH amplicon sequencing to characterize the functional potential and transcriptional activity of soil microbiomes. Before coming to SLU, I completed a bachelor’s degree in Ecology at Guangxi University (China), where I studied diazotrophic communities in double-rice paddies.
Outside the lab, I am an enthusiastic birder and have contributed to camera trap monitoring in mangrove reserves and avian biodiversity baseline surveys in southern China.
